anchor: On either side the river lie
title: The Lady of Shalott: versions and sources
short: First published in Poems (1832, dated 1833) and heavily revised for Poems (1842); this archive prints the 1842 text.
body: This is one of Tennyson's earliest Arthurian poems (a fragment, 'Sir Launcelot and Queen Guinevere', had appeared in 1830). The first version (20 stanzas) appeared in the volume dated 1833 but issued in December 1832; the revised text printed here (19 stanzas) appeared in 1842. Tennyson is said to have taken the name from an Italian novella, 'La Donna di Scalotta' (Il Novellino, no. 82), in which a maiden dies of love for Lancelot and floats down to Camelot in a boat. 'Shalott' is a form of the Astolat of the romances; Malory tells the related story of Elaine, the Fair Maid of Astolat, which Tennyson retold in 'Lancelot and Elaine' (1859). The isolation in the tower, the web, the mirror and the curse are Tennyson's additions.

sources.cite: H. M. McLuhan, ed., 'The Lady of Shalott (1842)', Representative Poetry Online (University of Toronto), line notes
'The Lady of Shalott', Wikipedia (citing Il Novellino LXXXII; Staines; Poulson)
Christopher Ricks, ed., The Poems of Tennyson, 2nd edn, 3 vols (Longman, 1987), headnote and line notes

title: wold
short: An open stretch of high, rolling country; Tennyson grew up in the Lincolnshire Wolds.
body: 'Wold' (Old English wald, forest) came to mean an area of open upland, as in the Cotswolds and the Lincolnshire Wolds, where Tennyson was born (Somersby). The fields of barley and rye 'clothe' the hills up to the skyline, an image of abundant, ordinary, working life that frames the enclosed island. Part I keeps returning to this busy outer world of roads, barges and reapers.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'wold' n.
Christopher Ricks, ed., The Poems of Tennyson, 2nd edn, 3 vols (Longman, 1987), headnote and line notes

title: Camelot
short: King Arthur's capital, whose location the romances leave uncertain; here a distant city of towers.
body: Camelot is the court of King Arthur in the romances. RPO notes that Caxton, in his preface to Malory, puts it in Wales; Malory himself identifies it with Winchester. Tennyson keeps it vague, a towered city downstream. Every stanza turns on the rhyme between 'Camelot' (line 5) and 'Shalott' (line 9), so the two places are fixed as the poles of the poem: the world of action and society, and the island of seclusion.

sources.cite: H. M. McLuhan, ed., 'The Lady of Shalott (1842)', Representative Poetry Online (University of Toronto), line notes
Thomas Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, ed. Caxton (1485), Preface and Book II, Project Gutenberg

title: stanza form and refrain
short: Nine-line stanzas rhymed aaaabcccb, mainly in iambic tetrameter, each ending on 'Camelot' and 'Shalott'.
body: Each stanza has four lines on one rhyme, a shorter fifth line ending 'Camelot', three more on a new rhyme, and a ninth line ending 'Shalott' (usually 'The Lady of Shalott'). The lines are mostly iambic tetrameter, with trimeter in the refrain lines. The long runs of a single rhyme ('lie / rye / sky / by') and the fixed refrains create a hypnotic, enclosed movement, like the weaving itself, and make any departure, such as the river's 'For ever' or the curse's arrival, felt strongly. The form is a ballad-like lyric with roots in medieval romance and in contemporary ballad imitation.

sources.cite: 'The Lady of Shalott', Wikipedia (citing Il Novellino LXXXII; Staines; Poulson)
H. M. McLuhan, ed., 'The Lady of Shalott (1842)', Representative Poetry Online (University of Toronto), line notes

title: shallop
short: A light open boat; it skims past 'unhail'd', with no one greeting it.
body: A shallop (from French chaloupe) is a small light boat. The stanza contrasts heavy barges dragged by 'slow horses' with the quick silken-sailed shallop, but both pass by without contact: 'unhail'd' means not greeted. The three questions that follow ('who hath seen her...?') make the Lady unknown to the passing world, preparing the moment when she herself becomes a boat drifting to Camelot.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'shallop' n.
Christopher Ricks, ed., The Poems of Tennyson, 2nd edn, 3 vols (Longman, 1987), headnote and line notes

title: the reapers
short: Only labourers hear her song; they take her for a fairy, which turns her into local legend.
body: The Lady is known only by sound: reapers at dawn and the tired reaper at night hear her singing and whisper that this is the 'fairy / Lady of Shalott'. The 'bearded barley' (barley has long bristles, or awns) and moonlit sheaves place her among the rhythms of rural work, but she remains invisible. The unusual feminine rhymes ('early / barley / cheerly / clearly') make the stanza sing. Critics who read the poem as an allegory of the artist note that her art reaches the world only indirectly and is misunderstood as enchantment.

sources.cite: 'The Lady of Shalott', Wikipedia (citing Il Novellino LXXXII; Staines; Poulson)
Christopher Ricks, ed., The Poems of Tennyson, 2nd edn, 3 vols (Longman, 1987), headnote and line notes

anchor: A magic web with colours gay
title: the magic web
short: She weaves a tapestry of what she sees; weaving is both her art and her imprisonment.
body: Weaving women are an ancient figure: Penelope at her loom, the Fates spinning destiny, Homer's Helen weaving the battles of Troy (Iliad III.125-128). The Lady's 'magic web' records the world in images, so it is often read as an emblem of art, especially art made in isolation. She weaves 'steadily' because of a curse whose nature she does not know, a condition many readers relate to the Victorian poet's uncertainty about engaging with society. David Staines, cited by Wikipedia, sees in the poem the study of the artist and the dangers of personal isolation; feminist critics read the enclosure as a picture of the confined Victorian woman.

sources.cite: 'The Lady of Shalott', Wikipedia (citing Il Novellino LXXXII; Staines; Poulson)
Homer, Iliad III.125-128 (Greek text and A. T. Murray trans., Perseus Digital Library)
Christopher Ricks, ed., The Poems of Tennyson, 2nd edn, 3 vols (Longman, 1987), headnote and line notes

title: the mirror
short: She may see the world only reflected in a mirror; the reflections are 'shadows', not realities.
body: Because she must not look directly at Camelot, the Lady watches the road and river in a mirror and weaves what it shows. The phrase 'Shadows of the world' invites comparison with Plato's allegory of the cave, where prisoners see only shadows of real things on a wall (Republic VII, 514a-517a). Tennyson's own later comment, recorded in the Memoir and quoted by RPO, said that her new-born love for someone in the wide world takes her out of the region of shadows into that of realities. The mirror is thus both protection and limitation.

sources.cite: H. M. McLuhan, ed., 'The Lady of Shalott (1842)', Representative Poetry Online (University of Toronto), line notes
Plato, Republic VII.514a-517a, Perseus Digital Library
Hallam Tennyson, Alfred Lord Tennyson: A Memoir, 2 vols (Macmillan, 1897)

title: pad
short: An easy-paced riding horse.
body: RPO glosses 'pad' as an easy-paced horse; the OED derives the word from 'pad-nag', a horse for the road (from Dutch or Low German pad, path). 'Ambling' describes its smooth gait, in which both legs on one side move together. The stanza lists the medieval figures who pass the mirror, damsels, an abbot, a shepherd, a page, knights, a social panorama of the world she cannot join.

sources.cite: H. M. McLuhan, ed., 'The Lady of Shalott (1842)', Representative Poetry Online (University of Toronto), line notes
Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'pad' n.3

title: churls
short: Peasants, rustics; by Tennyson's time the word also implied rudeness.
body: 'Churl' (Old English ceorl, a free man of the lowest rank) came to mean a peasant and then a rude, ill-bred person (OED). 'Surly' strengthens the later sense. The village churls and the 'red cloaks of market girls' bring colour and ordinary life into the mirror, and they 'Pass onward from Shalott': the outside world is always moving, while she remains.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'churl' n.
Christopher Ricks, ed., The Poems of Tennyson, 2nd edn, 3 vols (Longman, 1987), headnote and line notes

anchor: I am half sick of shadows
title: 'I am half sick of shadows'
short: The turning point: a funeral and newly married lovers in the mirror make her weary of seeing life at second hand.
body: The stanza sets death (a funeral 'with plumes and lights') beside love ('two young lovers lately wed'), the two great events she cannot share. Her words are the first she speaks and the end of Part II. 'Half sick' is exact: she is not yet in revolt, only tired. In the 1832 version the line is the same, which shows it was central from the start. J. W. Waterhouse took it as the title of his 1915 painting, and Tennyson's own gloss on love leading 'out of the region of shadows' (Memoir I, 116-17, quoted by RPO) is usually applied here.

sources.cite: H. M. McLuhan, ed., 'The Lady of Shalott (1842)', Representative Poetry Online (University of Toronto), line notes
'The Lady of Shalott (1832)', Representative Poetry Online (University of Toronto)
'The Lady of Shalott', Wikipedia (citing Il Novellino LXXXII; Staines; Poulson)

title: brazen greaves
short: Bronze armour for the shins, a Homeric piece of equipment given to a medieval knight.
body: Greaves are pieces of armour covering the leg below the knee (OED). 'Brazen' (of brass or bronze) makes them recall the bronze-greaved Achaeans of the Iliad, whose standard epithet is 'well-greaved' (euknemides). The sun 'flamed' on them: Part III is a blaze of light and metal after the grey, shadowed world of Parts I-II. 'Bower-eaves' are the eaves of her chamber ('bower', a lady's private room).

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'greave' n. and 'bower' n.1
Homer, Iliad I.17 (euknemides Achaioi) (Greek text and A. T. Murray trans., Perseus Digital Library)

title: Sir Lancelot
short: The greatest knight of Arthur's court and Queen Guinevere's lover; in the Astolat story, the man the maiden loves.
body: Lancelot du Lac is the pre-eminent knight of the Round Table, whose love for Guinevere eventually destroys Arthur's fellowship (Malory). In Malory's story of the Fair Maid of Astolat (Book XVIII), Elaine loves him, he cannot return her love, and she dies and is sent to Camelot in a barge. Here Lancelot does not know the Lady exists: all of Part III is description of his dazzling appearance as she sees it, which makes her turn an act of desire for something glimpsed rather than a response to any man's attention.

sources.cite: Thomas Malory, Le Morte d'Arthur, Book XVIII, chs. 9-20, Project Gutenberg
'The Lady of Shalott', Wikipedia (citing Il Novellino LXXXII; Staines; Poulson)

title: A red-cross knight for ever kneel'd
short: His shield shows a knight in a red cross kneeling to a lady, an emblem of courtly devotion and an echo of Spenser.
body: The device on Lancelot's shield shows a knight wearing the red cross (St George's emblem, and the badge of Spenser's Redcrosse Knight, The Faerie Queene I.i.2) kneeling forever to a lady. It is an image of courtly love and religious chivalry, frozen in art, like the Lady's own woven images. The irony is that Lancelot's devotion belongs to Guinevere, not to the Lady who watches; the 'yellow field' is both the heraldic gold ground of the shield and the ripe barley around him.

sources.cite: Edmund Spenser, The Faerie Queene I.i.2 (1590), Project Gutenberg
Christopher Ricks, ed., The Poems of Tennyson, 2nd edn, 3 vols (Longman, 1987), headnote and line notes

title: Galaxy
short: The Milky Way; the jewelled bridle shines like a branch of stars.
body: RPO glosses 'Galaxy' as the Milky Way. The word comes from Greek galaxias, 'milky', from gala, milk, the name for the band of stars across the night sky. The simile is part of the poem's cosmic scale for Lancelot: his bridle is like a branch of stars, his helmet-feather burns like a flame, and he passes like a meteor. The Lady sees him as a celestial apparition rather than a man.

sources.cite: H. M. McLuhan, ed., 'The Lady of Shalott (1842)', Representative Poetry Online (University of Toronto), line notes
Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'galaxy' n.

title: blazon'd baldric
short: A belt worn across the shoulder to carry a sword or horn, decorated with heraldic devices.
body: A baldric is a belt worn from one shoulder to the opposite hip, used to hang a sword or, here, a 'mighty silver bugle' (a hunting horn). 'Blazon'd' means painted or embroidered with heraldic arms (OED, 'blazon'). The alliteration of b-sounds ('bridle bells', 'blazon'd baldric', 'bugle') and the bells and ringing armour make the stanza noisy and bright, the opposite of the silent island.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'baldric' n. and 'blazon' v.
Christopher Ricks, ed., The Poems of Tennyson, 2nd edn, 3 vols (Longman, 1987), headnote and line notes

title: bearded meteor
short: A comet or shooting star with a trailing tail; comets were omens of change and disaster.
body: 'Bearded' translates the old way of describing comets by their tails (Greek kometes means 'long-haired'; OED 'comet'). In the nineteenth century 'meteor' could include any bright atmospheric or celestial phenomenon. Comets were traditionally omens: 'Comets, importing change of times and states' opens 1 Henry VI. Lancelot's passing is a portent for the Lady, foreshadowing the catastrophe that follows; the simile also emphasises his remoteness, crossing 'still Shalott' without stopping.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'comet' n. and 'meteor' n.
Shakespeare, 1 Henry VI I.i.2 (Folger Shakespeare Library text)

title: Tirra lirra
short: A carefree refrain borrowed from Autolycus's song in The Winter's Tale.
body: RPO notes the source in Shakespeare's The Winter's Tale (IV.iii), where the rogue Autolycus sings of 'The lark, that tirra-lyra chants'. The nonsense refrain marks Lancelot's light-heartedness: he sings as he rides, unaware of the effect he has. It is the only thing the Lady hears from him before she leaves the loom. The double 'river' rhyme ('river / mirror / river') sets him visually and aurally into her mirror world.

sources.cite: H. M. McLuhan, ed., 'The Lady of Shalott (1842)', Representative Poetry Online (University of Toronto), line notes
Shakespeare, The Winter's Tale IV.iii (Folger Shakespeare Library text)

title: the mirror crack'd
short: The climax: she leaves the loom, looks directly at Camelot, and the web flies out and the mirror breaks.
body: The stanza moves through five short clauses beginning 'She': left, made, saw, saw, look'd. The repetition makes her action decisive and ritual-like. Then the consequences arrive in impersonal verbs: the web flies out, the mirror cracks, the curse comes. Looking directly at the world destroys both her art (the web) and her means of seeing (the mirror). The line became proverbial (Agatha Christie's novel The Mirror Crack'd from Side to Side, 1962). Readers differ on whether her choice is a fall, a liberation, or both; Christine Poulson, cited in Wikipedia, reads the escape as defiance and female empowerment.

sources.cite: 'The Lady of Shalott', Wikipedia (citing Il Novellino LXXXII; Staines; Poulson)
Christopher Ricks, ed., The Poems of Tennyson, 2nd edn, 3 vols (Longman, 1987), headnote and line notes

title: Like some bold seër in a trance
short: Like a prophet seeing his own doom, she gazes toward Camelot with a fixed, glassy face.
body: The diaeresis in 'seër' marks two syllables: a seer is one who sees visions. The simile compares her to a prophet in a trance who foresees his own 'mischance' (misfortune) and cannot avert it. 'Glassy countenance' suggests a fixed, unblinking look, and also turns her face into a kind of mirror now that the real one is broken. The storm stanza before it (east wind, waning woods, raining sky) is the poem's only bad weather, matching her fate.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'seer' n.1 and 'mischance' n.
Christopher Ricks, ed., The Poems of Tennyson, 2nd edn, 3 vols (Longman, 1987), headnote and line notes

anchor: round about the prow she wrote
title: her name on the prow
short: She writes her name on the boat, turning herself into a text that Camelot will read.
body: The woman who has been known only as a rumour now identifies herself in writing. The detail completes a pattern in which she becomes her own work of art: robed in white, singing her 'last song', she drifts downstream like the funeral she once watched in the mirror. In the Italian novella the dead maiden carries a letter; Tennyson transfers the message to the boat. At the end the people 'read her name' on the prow, the only thing they can know of her.

sources.cite: 'The Lady of Shalott', Wikipedia (citing Il Novellino LXXXII; Staines; Poulson)
H. M. McLuhan, ed., 'The Lady of Shalott (1842)', Representative Poetry Online (University of Toronto), line notes

anchor: A corse between the houses high
title: corse
short: An archaic, poetic form of 'corpse'.
body: 'Corse' is an older form of 'corpse' (from Latin corpus, body), kept in poetry for its solemn and archaic sound (OED). The stanza shows the boat entering the city 'silent', a 'gleaming shape' passing balcony and gallery. The contrast with the noisy, bright Lancelot of Part III is pointed: she arrives at Camelot only as a body, and the court's festive 'royal cheer' dies at the sight.

sources.cite: Oxford English Dictionary, s.v. 'corse' n.
Christopher Ricks, ed., The Poems of Tennyson, 2nd edn, 3 vols (Longman, 1987), headnote and line notes

title: Lancelot's last words
short: Added in 1842: Lancelot's brief response, read as tender, as shallow, or as deliberately understated.
body: In the 1832 version the poem ended with the townsfolk finding a parchment on her breast, which announced that the web was woven, the charm broken, and 'this is I, / The Lady of Shalott'. In 1842 Tennyson replaced this with Lancelot's musing, a change that ends the poem on the man she saw rather than on her own statement. Some readers find his words merely aesthetic, a comment on her face that repeats the world's failure to know her; others hear genuine pity in the prayer 'God in his mercy lend her grace'. The irony is that Lancelot, the cause of her death, never learns it.
